profiles.name: Zurebu Gardner
profiles.description: Zurebu Gardner was a Black community activist in Riverside, California, one of two men charged with the April 1971 murder of two Riverside police officers — a prosecution his supporters, organized as the Riverside Political Prisoners Defense Committee, denounced as a frame-up. By 1974 Lawton and Gardner had been tried twice, with both trials ending in hung juries (reportedly 11 to 1 for acquittal), and a third trial was pending; the case never produced a conviction. Documented in The Black Panther (April 13, 1974).
profiles.query: "Zurebu Gardner" Riverside Lawton1971 photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Freedom Archives Lawton case coverage found; no verified Gardner portrait.

profiles.name: Pablo "Yoruba" Guzmán
profiles.description: Pablo "Yoruba" Guzmán was Minister of Information of the New York Young Lords and was arrested in the group's 1969–70 direct actions, including the occupation of the First Spanish Methodist Church in East Harlem and the takeover of Lincoln Hospital. He later became an Emmy-winning New York broadcast journalist.
profiles.query: "Pablo Yoruba Guzmán" Young Lords journalist photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Museum of City of New York and Northwestern captioned Young Lords group photos; CBS obituary independently confirms journalist identity. Original image/crop verification pending.

profiles.name: Hector Marroquin
profiles.description:
Héctor Marroquín was a Mexican-born activist whose decade-long fight against deportation became a major political-asylum and civil-liberties cause championed by the U.S. left. Born in Matamoros, Mexico, he came to the United States in 1974 and became active in the antideportation and trade-union movements and a member of the Young Socialist Alliance and the Socialist Workers Party. He said he had fled political persecution in Mexico — where he was wanted in connection with the student and leftist movements — and feared torture or death if he were returned.

In September 1977, returning from a visit to Mexico, Marroquín was detained by the Immigration and Naturalization Service at Eagle Pass, Texas and charged with entering the country illegally; he applied for political asylum. A Héctor Marroquín Defense Committee organized national support, and his testimony featured in the SWP's landmark Socialist Workers Party v. Attorney General lawsuit over FBI and government surveillance of the left. After roughly eleven years of government efforts to deport him for his political activity, Marroquín ultimately won the right to remain in the United States.
profiles.query: "Hector Marroquin" SWP asylum photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Militant1978 issue23 captioned portrait credited Susan Ellis; defense pamphlet cover also lead. Scan extraction pending.

profiles.name: Tess Ewing
profiles.description: Tess Ewing was a Boston school-bus driver and member of the United Steelworkers (USWA) who was jailed for contempt during the union's strike in the spring of 1977. When the drivers struck in April 1977, a court issued a no-strike injunction; Ewing was among those jailed for defying it, serving twelve days at the Framingham Women's Correctional Institution. She saw the jailings as part of an effort, as she put it, "to squeeze out a contract" from the union.
profiles.query: "Tess Ewing" Boston bus driver1977 photograph portrait
profiles.finding: UMass Boston Tess Ewing collection and Militant1978 strike account corroborate identity; no individual portrait verified.

profiles.name: Wilford Davis
profiles.description: Wilford Davis was a Black prisoner in Washington State, convicted of murder and serving a life sentence. He had been shot in the spine and paralyzed from the waist down at Oroville on November 28, 1974; after his April 1975 conviction he was sent to the Washington Corrections Center at Shelton, where the specialized medical care his paralysis required was withdrawn. He filed suit seeking $125,000 in damages over the inhumane denial of medical care. Documented in The Black Panther (July 24, 1976).
profiles.query: "Wilford Davis" Washington Shelton prisoner photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Shelton prisoner-specific search did not establish portrait.

profiles.name: Dave Smith
profiles.description: Dave Smith, born about 1946 on a Texas dirt farm, joined the United States Army at 17 and became a Russian-language specialist. As his opposition to the Vietnam War grew, he accumulated disciplinary trouble. In 1969 he went absent without leave for 30 days, served six months in the Army stockade and was reduced to private. When ordered to Da Nang, Smith instead traveled under a friend’s name to Denmark and then Sweden, where he received humanitarian asylum and later became a Swedish citizen. Exact stockade entry and release dates have not been located.
profiles.query: "Dave Smith" Sweden deserter Vietnam photograph portrait
profiles.finding: 1982 Washington Post Swedish resister account found. NZ photo and U.S. Marine Dave Smith lack identity match.

profiles.name: Richard Johnstone
profiles.description: Richard Johnstone, born about 1944 and raised on a farm near Brooklyn, Iowa, was a graduate music student when the United States Army drafted him in 1970. Four weeks into basic training at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri, he left the Army and traveled to Sweden. Johnstone worked as a rehearsal pianist at the Stockholm ballet. The Army formally released him in 1977 under the Carter administration’s program for deserters, giving him a general discharge and the ability to visit the United States. The reviewed sources do not report any arrest, booking or confinement.
profiles.query: "Richard Johnstone" Sweden pianist deserter photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Washington Post Swedish deserter/pianist account found; no portrait verified.

profiles.name: William Schiller
profiles.description: William “Bill” Schiller was an early Peace Corps volunteer who became an opponent of the Vietnam War after the United States intervened in the Dominican Republic and escalated in Vietnam. He mailed his draft card to the Selective Service System and left the United States, reaching Sweden in 1970. Schiller received humanitarian asylum, became a Swedish citizen and was working as an English-language radio reporter in Stockholm in 1982. The reviewed sources do not report an arrest, booking or confinement.
profiles.query: "William Schiller" Sweden Peace Corps radio photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Washington Post Swedish asylum/radio context found; no portrait verified.

profiles.name: Anthony Williams
profiles.description: Anthony "Tony" Williams was an Attica prisoner prosecuted after the September 1971 uprising. Attica News documented two months in Erie County Jail on the resulting indictment before its dismissal was announced in February 1973. A later notice by fellow prisoner Akil identified Williams by his full name and reported that he had died at Great Meadow Correctional Facility in Comstock, New York. The notice said the writers learned of his death on June 19, 1975; his actual death date remains unverified.

profiles.finding: Attica/Comstock1975 search did not establish identity-linked portrait.

profiles.name: Tom Forcade
profiles.description: Tom Forcade was also known as Thomas King Forcade and Kenneth Gary Goodson and oversaw the Underground Press Syndicate and founded High Times. Following the 1972 Miami political conventions, he faced a federal explosives prosecution. Albert Goldman's retrospective describes his confinement in a guarded jail cell; Forcade's later interview dates his acquittal to 1973. The surviving accounts reviewed do not establish exact custody dates or time served.
profiles.query: "Tom Forcade" High Times founder photograph portrait
profiles.finding: High Times institutional history has founder photo leads; original asset and credit pending.

profiles.name: Carlos Calderon
profiles.description: Carlos Calderon was a Brown Beret and an editor of El Barrio, a section of San Diego's Street Journal. He was one of Los Tres de San Diego prosecuted in 1970–71. A San Diego Reader history records actual confinement and release after newspaper colleagues raised bail. Accounts disagree about the prosecution's final outcome, so his individual disposition and exact custody duration remain unresolved.
profiles.query: "Carlos Calderon" San Diego Brown Beret photograph portrait
profiles.finding: San Diego Brown Beret-specific search did not verify portrait.

profiles.name: Jerome Friedman
profiles.description: Jerome 'Jerry' Friedman was Ohio State's undergraduate student president in 1971–72, an antiwar activist, and executive director of the Columbus Community Union. In May 1972 he was jailed under $100,000 bail. The reviewing court reduced it to $10,000, finding it unreasonable and discussing the original judge's objection to Friedman's criticism at a political meeting. His exact release date and final criminal disposition remain unverified.
profiles.query: "Jerome Friedman" Ohio State student1972 photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Ohio State1972 case-specific search did not verify portrait; Nobel physicist not accepted.

profiles.name: Colin Neiburger
profiles.description: Colin Neiburger participated in the Columbus antiwar movement of the 1970s. A May 1972 court opinion documents his detention under $100,000 bail and reduces the bond to $10,000 as excessive. The opinion also discusses earlier violence-related matters; the bail ruling did not determine the pending charges. His exact confinement interval and final disposition remain unverified.

profiles.finding: Columbus1972 antiwar query did not verify portrait.

profiles.name: Ron Ridenour
profiles.description: Ron Ridenour was a Los Angeles Free Press journalist and supporter of striking Chicana garment workers. He was arrested at a picket line in November 1970 and convicted of resisting arrest. The Militant reported in November 1973 that he was serving a six-month jail sentence on nights and weekends while allowed to work weekdays. The newspaper characterized the prosecution as a frame-up. This strike-support case was distinct from his later prosecution for photographing police at an antiwar protest.
profiles.query: "Ron Ridenour" Free Press journalist photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Own biography corroborates LA Free Press and six-month confinement; own portrait only72x101 and rejected as too small. Mississippi1964 arrest photograph in Civil Rights Digital Library remains lead.

profiles.name: Steven Abbott
profiles.description: Steven Abbott was a Columbus Free Press writer jailed in 1972 on riot-related misdemeanor charges. In Abbott v. City of Columbus, the reviewing court found no justification for his $20,000 bail and reduced it to $3,000. The state's adverse character evidence consisted of an article attributed to him, while the original bail decision had treated his charges as a felony. The opinion establishes actual detention but not its length or the final criminal outcome.
profiles.query: "Steven Abbott" Columbus Free Press1972 photograph portrait
profiles.finding: Columbus Free Press1972 query did not verify portrait.

profiles.name: Kent Hoffman
profiles.description:
Kent Hoffman was a Catholic Worker who was imprisoned with Jeff Dietrich following a nonviolent protest at a Military Arms Bazaar in October 1979. A 1983 Nuclear Resister review of Dietrich’s prison writings reports that both men were released after serving 59 days when the judge reduced an unusually harsh sentence following public criticism.

Sources: https://media.nukeresister.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/NR015_19830309small.pdf#page=16

profiles.finding: Sun Magazine Reluctant Resister and NCR Catholic Worker history found; no portrait verified.
